source: ACIAR Monograph No. 146a, "ដំណាំសំណែកសៀង" [Soybean Growers Manual], Belfield S., Brown C., Martin M. (eds.), New South Wales Department of Primary Industries / Murdoch University / CARDI / ACIAR, 2012
text:
The manual's IPM/pest chapter profiles the same core soybean pest complex found across this batch's other soybean sources, each with photos, identification notes, and management notes: soybean aphid (Aphis glycines Matsumura, sucking sap from young leaves/stems/pods, transmitting some viruses); green stink bug (Nezara viridula, feeding on developing pods and causing shrivelled/discolored seed); leaf webworm (Stomopteryx subsecivella, larvae web and skeletonize leaves); coreid bugs (Riptortus linearis and R. serripes, feeding on pods); bruchid weevils (Callosobruchus chinensis and C. maculatus, a storage pest that infests seed after harvest); cutworm and earwig as soil/stem-level pests; and beneficial predators including a six-spotted ladybird beetle (Cheilomenes sexmaculata) which the manual specifically flags as a natural aphid predator worth conserving through selective, threshold-based spraying rather than blanket insecticide use.

The manual gives a resistance-management framework tied to reproductive growth stage — different insecticide chemical classes are recommended in rotation across R1–R2, R3–R4, and R4–R5 windows specifically to slow the development of pesticide resistance in the pest population, rather than using the same product repeatedly through the season.
